summary: Offers advice on advertising over email and newsgroups without annoying the people who receive it. It argues that responsible, targeted, honest marketing works better than blasting unwanted messages. The memo is informational guidance, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: Don't shout your ads at everyone in the street. If you politely tell only people who want to hear, they will stay your friends.

questions: how to advertise responsibly by email
subtitle: Guidelines for ethical email and newsgroup marketing

tldr.problem: Unsolicited bulk email (spam) and irresponsible marketing damage both advertiser reputation and the Internet community. Marketers who spam face legal action, lost connectivity, and market backlash.
tldr.mechanism: Advertisers should target only genuinely interested recipients through opt-in mailing lists, responsible posting to appropriate newsgroups, and websites. The key is knowing the audience and respecting their choice to receive advertisements.
tldr.outcome: Responsible advertising benefits everyone: advertisers maintain credibility and avoid legal trouble, recipients see only relevant offers, and the Internet remains a useful medium for commerce.

facts.label: Opt-in email effectiveness
facts.value: 18 percent more effective than banner advertising

today: RFC 3098 was published in April 2001 as practical guidance for Internet advertisers. The advice remains sound: opt-in marketing, reputation management, and respecting recipient choice are still the foundation of legitimate email marketing. The RFC serves as a historical reminder of early 2000s email abuse problems and the ethical principles that evolved from that era. Anti-spam legislation like the CAN-SPAM Act (United States, 2003) and GDPR (European Union, 2018) later codified many of these principles into law.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 3098 offers practical guidance on responsible advertising through email and newsgroups. The RFC addresses a critical problem: many new Internet businesses send bulk unsolicited email (spam) to reach millions of people cheaply, not realizing the true costs and consequences.

The Internet standards that enable open communication were designed before spam existed. Because sending a million emails costs almost nothing, marketers have shifted the burden to recipients, who pay in bandwidth, storage, and time. This condition has created strong opposition to unsolicited bulk email across the Internet community.

The RFC argues that responsible, targeted marketing is more effective and sustainable than broadcasting to uninterested parties.
sections.eli5: This document explains why sending ads to everyone is bad for everyone, and shows a smarter way to advertise on the Internet that actually works.

sections.title: The Cost of Spam and the Image Problem
sections.content:
Spamming harms the advertiser. Unsolicited mass email alienates the vast majority of recipients, damages credibility, and often violates ISP policies (which typically have strict zero-tolerance anti-spam rules). In many jurisdictions, sending spam can result in civil or criminal litigation; courts have recognized spam as a form of trespass to chattels (unauthorized use of property) and have awarded damages.

The Internet renders everyone anonymous, so reputation, honesty, and integrity are the only tools an online business has to build trust. An advertiser broadcasting to millions of uninterested parties becomes a "spammer" and thief in the eyes of the community.

The RFC also discusses collateral damage: spammers often forge email headers or relay messages through third-party systems to hide their identity. These practices are criminal in many countries and breach the laws of multiple jurisdictions.
sections.eli5: Spammers face death threats, lawsuits, and losing their Internet access. People online judge you by your reputation, so spam destroys your business.

sections.title: Finding the Right Audience
sections.content:
Before advertising, an advertiser must determine the appropriate channels and the right audience for each specific advertisement.

For newsgroups, check the FAQ to see if the group welcomes advertising, ask the group's moderator, or read the group for a while to understand the culture. Never assume blind broadcasting is acceptable.

For email lists, understand that compiled third-party mailing lists are problematic. List providers often gather addresses unethically: scraping outdated archives, using dictionary attacks to generate invalid addresses, or even selling lists of people who requested removal. Purchasing such a list shifts the maintenance burden to the advertiser and exposes them to liability.

The safest and most effective approach is for the advertiser to build their own list through an opt-in process where potential customers affirmatively choose to receive marketing messages.
sections.eli5: Find where people who want your product hang out, ask permission first, and never buy a list of email addresses from a stranger.

sections.title: Opt-In Mailing Lists
sections.content:
Opt-in mailing lists are far more effective than any other form of Internet advertising. Studies show opt-in email is 18 percent more effective than banner advertising, because the recipients affirmatively signed up to receive the information.

When building an opt-in list, three principles matter:

  • Privacy: People must know data is being collected and for what purpose. Offer a clear checkbox for opting in (with opt-in as the default, not opt-out). Different jurisdictions have different privacy laws; the advertiser bears the responsibility to understand them.
  • Integrity: Verify subscriptions by sending a confirmation email listing the subscribed address, date, time, method of subscription, IP address, and clear unsubscribe instructions. This protects both the advertiser and the legitimate subscriber from fraud.
  • Protection: Keep archives of all subscription requests to defend against false spam complaints. These records should be safeguarded as carefully as any business records.
sections.eli5: Ask people if they want to hear from you, tell them exactly what you are doing, and keep records so you can prove they said yes.

sections.title: What to Do and Not to Do
sections.content:
DO NOT:

  • Forge email headers to hide the sender's identity or origin
  • Send fake "accidental" messages designed to advertise while looking like personal notes
  • Create mailing lists from third-party sources or purchased lists
  • Sell mailing lists that customers trusted you with

DO:

  • Create a dedicated website or place ads on legitimate shared advertising sites
  • Participate in mailing lists and newsgroups relevant to your product, being helpful rather than purely self-promotional
  • Use short, honest email signatures (4 lines maximum)
  • Respect customer privacy by keeping lists private and encrypting sensitive information
  • Make unsubscribing as easy as subscribing, and include unsubscribe instructions in every message
  • Tell recipients exactly how and why you collected their data
sections.eli5: Be honest, be helpful, ask permission, make it easy to leave, and never pretend to be someone you are not.

left.title: Irresponsible
left.desc: Broadcast ads to millions of uninterested strangers, forging headers, buying spam lists, facing lawsuits and disconnection.

right.title: Responsible
right.desc: Target interested people who requested information, respect their privacy, maintain reputation and customer relationships.
